newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's NSW govt defends Sydney hotel tax.
newsitem.headline: Australia's NSW govt defends Sydney hotel tax.

text.p: New South Wales Treasurer Michael Egan said on Wednesday he would not apologise to the tourist and hotel industry for the 10 percent hotel tax the state government introduced in its budget for 1997/98 (July-June).
Egan told a breakfast function presenting the budget that wealthy overseas tourists took advantage of Sydney's roads, public transport and other infrastructure and could afford to pay extra for that.
He said the hotel industry had boomed in recent years and was expected to continue booming in the lead up to the Olympics.

He said the state government planned to spend A$628.1 million on construction of Olympic facilities over 1997/98 as part of plans to spend a total A$2.1 billion of government money on Olympic projects by 2000.
"I make no apology for expecting people who visit Sydney to pay some of that cost," Egan said.
The 10 percent accomodation duty applies to hotels, motels, and guest houses in and around the Sydney Central Business District.
It was projected to eventually raise A$64 million a year.
Hotel operators and tourism authorities have reacted angrily to the tax, saying it will discourage new development.
The Tourism Council of Australia has also said it would challenge the tax in court, arguing it was unconstitutional for a state government to raise such a tax.
